title: Book 3 — Thalia, Chapter 449
paragraphs: At last Periander made a proclamation that whoever should either receive him into their houses or converse with him would be bound to pay a fine to Apollo, and he stated the amount. Accordingly, because of this proclamation, no one was willing either to converse with him or receive him into their house; and moreover he himself did not think it right even to try, since it had been forbidden, but he lay about in the porticoes enduring exposure. On the fourth day after this, Periander, seeing him fallen into squalid misery and starvation, felt pity for him, and abating his anger he approached him and began to say: “Son, which of these two is to be preferred: the fortune you now experience and possess, or to inherit the power and wealth I now possess, by being submissive to your father's will? You, however, being my son and the prince of wealthy Corinth, chose nevertheless the life of a vagabond by making opposition and showing anger against the one with whom it least behooved you to deal so. For if any misfortune happened in those matters, on account of which you hold suspicion against me, it has happened to me first, and I am a sharer in the misfortune more than others, inasmuch as I did the deed myself. Since you have learned, then, how much better it is to be envied than to be pitied, and at the same time what a grievous thing it is to be angry against your parents and against those stronger than you, come back now to the house.” With these words Periander tried to restrain him; but he answered his father nothing else but that he ought to pay a fine to the god for having come to speech with him. Then Periander, perceiving that his son's malady was hopeless and could not be overcome, sent a ship to Corcyra and sent him away out of his sight, for he was ruler of that island too; and having sent him away, Periander proceeded to make war against his father-in-law Procles, holding him most to blame for his condition, and he took Epidauros and took Procles himself prisoner.
